title: Renal colic and the obstructed infected kidney
subtitle: Infection behind a stone: decompress first

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management (NG118)
EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections: urosepsis
Surviving Sepsis Campaign: international guidelines for management of sepsis and septic shock 2021

red_flags.text: Fever, rigors or sepsis with a ureteric stone or hydronephrosis: an obstructed infected kidney. This is a urological emergency.
Acute kidney injury, anuria, a solitary or transplanted kidney, or bilateral obstruction.
Pain that does not settle with adequate analgesia.
An older patient with first-ever 'renal colic': exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm before accepting the diagnosis.

do_now.text: Obstruction with infection: arrange urgent decompression of the collecting system by percutaneous nephrostomy or retrograde ureteric stent. Both are effective; choose by local availability and the patient.
Take blood and urine cultures, then start empirical intravenous antibiotics per local protocol without waiting for imaging or theatre.
Defer definitive stone treatment until the infection has resolved. Ureteroscopy or lithotripsy in an infected obstructed system risks overwhelming sepsis.
Analgesia: offer a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug by any route as first line; intravenous paracetamol if it is contraindicated; opioids only if both are contraindicated or ineffective.

assess.text: Sepsis screen at the front door and repeated. Rigors, tachycardia and hypotension may appear before the fever.
Renal function and the presence of a single functioning kidney.
A clinical stone score can support the probability of an uncomplicated ureteric stone in a well patient, but it does not replace imaging when the diagnosis or complication is uncertain.
Pregnancy test in every woman of child-bearing age before imaging.

investigate.text: Low-dose non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder in adults with suspected colic, within 24 hours of presentation, and immediately when there is a fever, a solitary kidney, or diagnostic uncertainty.
Ultrasound first in pregnancy and in children and young people; low-dose CT only if ultrasound does not answer the question.
Full blood count, renal function, electrolytes, calcium, C-reactive protein, lactate, urine dipstick and culture, blood cultures if febrile.
Send the urine from the renal pelvis at decompression for culture; it often differs from the bladder urine.

resuscitate.text: Fluid resuscitation and vasopressors for septic shock per sepsis guidance; decompression is part of the resuscitation, not a step that follows it.
Admit to a level of care that matches the physiology. An obstructed infected kidney can deteriorate quickly after the first hours.

definitive.text: Uncomplicated colic with a small distal ureteric stone: consider an alpha-blocker as medical expulsive therapy, with follow-up imaging to confirm passage.

Stones unlikely to pass, uncontrolled pain, or obstruction with impaired function: ureteroscopy or shockwave lithotripsy, within 48 hours of diagnosis or admission when pain is ongoing and not tolerated, or the stone is unlikely to pass.
After decompression for infection: complete the antibiotic course, then plan definitive stone clearance electively.
Every stent is registered with a removal date. A forgotten stent encrusts and becomes its own operation.

escalate.text: Urology registrar and consultant immediately for an obstructed infected kidney.
Interventional radiology for nephrostomy, the same night if the patient is septic and retrograde stenting is not quickly available.
Critical care for septic shock. Vascular surgery if an aneurysm has not been excluded.

notes: Pus under pressure in the kidney is an abscess, and the treatment of an abscess is drainage. Antibiotics alone fail because they cannot reach an obstructed collecting system.
A stent and a nephrostomy are equally good at decompression. The better one is whichever can be done soonest and most safely for this patient tonight.
The dangerous trap is the well-looking patient with a small stone, a fever and a modest hydronephrosis. Small stones still obstruct, and the sepsis declares itself overnight.
